title: What Are Your Thoughts On Chimes At Midnight?

commenti.body: Its one of Welles greatest films and one of the best Shakespeare adaptations. Its top 3 Welles for me. Despite the nature of the production his genius and his craftmanship is on full display. The cast is excellent as well.

His best film after Citizen Kane. I think one of the biggest reasons why it isn't discussed more, is because in order to glean the highest amount of enjoyment from it, you'll need to have a thorough understanding of the 5 or 6 plays from which it's cobbled and rearranged from. If you can't understand the language, it's not even a matter of being able to judge whether it's good or bad, as the predominant feeling you'll have, above all, will be frustration. Otherwise, if you go in blind, you'll probably have to watch it multiple times until the dialogue becomes familiar (and practically memorized), but that will undoubtedly feel like too much work for many. 

Aside from that imposing barrier, it has a ton of things going for it. It naturally has great sets and one of the best medieval atmospheres I've ever seen captured in cinema (perhaps second to "Andrei Rublev" in my estimation). It has Welles's best directed action sequence in the Battle of Shrewsbury (which was an acknowledged influence on films like "Braveheart"), as well as the best acting performance by Welles in a film that he personally made. Perhaps most importantly though, it has a rare fluidity of vision--intact and untarnished--that I've only really felt in "Citizen Kane," "The Trial" and "F for Fake." It's easily in the top three best Shakespeare film adaptations ever made alongside Kurosawa's two masterpieces.

I had tried to watch it a couple of times long ago but just couldn't get into it (this was long before Criterion's lovely restoration). The language was a barrier and you kind of have to know the history/Shakespeare plays it's based on. 

However, after obsessively watching **The Hollow Crown** I was ready to tackle the Chimes at Midnight and I loved it.  Welles is able to bring so much life to the material, and compose his shots so that every frame is captivating, dynamic, and richly textured. He's also the perfect actor to play Falstaff. 

I was less in love with Keith Baxter's Prince Hal, who is like a cross between Anthony Perkins and Roddy MacDowell, but his character arc from wild youth to responsible king is done really well here. The realization of his responsibilities is palpable, as is Falstaff's fall from grace. 

Norman Rodway is terrific as Hotspur (a role originally intended for Brian Blessed - a shame he couldn't do it). John Gielgud gives us a commanding Henry IV whose sobriety contrasts well with Prince Hal's informality. Jeanne Moreau is wasted as Doll. 

Welles also manages, on a minuscule budget, to film a surprisingly violent and visceral battle scene that's a masterclass in Eisensteinian montage and is as good as any action movie battle today.

I highly recommend The Hollow Crown and following it up with Chimes at Midnight.
What special features on the Blu-Ray do you feel are particular standouts? I think I might have to pick it up.

The restoration itself makes it worth getting but the commentary by James Naremore is good and it has some great interviews with Keith Baxter, Beatrice Welles, Simon Callow and Joseph McBride. There's also an interview with Welles from while he was editing the film.

One of Orson Welles' best and least-seen movies. Those of us who resisted our teachers' best efforts to make us appreciate the comic genius of Shakespeare's fools and buffoons will not be surprised that Welles wasn't able to make Falstaff very funny; he's a great conception of a character, but the charades and practical jokes and the carousing and roistering seem meant to be funnier than they are. The movie does have a great Shakespearean comic moment, though: garrulous Falstaff sitting with Shallow (Alan Webb) and Silence (Walter Chiari), rolling his eyes in irritation and impatience at Silence's stammer. Though Welles' performance as Falstaff is short on comedy, it's very rich, very full. Oddly, we never really see the friendship of Falstaff and Prince Hal-played extraordinarily well by Keith Baxter-but John Gielgud's refined, monkish Henry IV gives the film the austerity it needs for the conflict within Hal to be dramatized. The film is a near-masterpiece. Welles' direction of the battle of Shrewsbury is unlike anything he has ever done-indeed, unlike any battle ever done on the screen before. It ranks with the finest of Griffith, John Ford, Eisenstein, Kurosawa. The compositions suggest Uccello, and the chilling, ironic music is a death knell for all men in battle. The soldiers, plastered by the mud they fall in, are already monuments. It's the most brutally sombre battle ever filmed, and it does justice to Hotspur's great "O, Harry, thou hast robbed me of my youth." 

#

This film is a masterpiece, and it is the greatest Shakespeare adaptation.

The purists might rage that it's technically an adaptation of parts of at least four plays (*Henry IV Part One*, *Henry IV Part Two*, *Henry V*, and *The Merry Wives of Windsor*) pivoting around a conceptual Falstaff fulcrum.

I can't imagine a better casting fit in proportion and spirit for Falstaff. It's such a careful, nuanced performance, particularly in the emotional climax. It's clear that Welles deeply understood the work he was adapting.

It had all sorts of well documented production issues, and there are technical glitches and odd corners, but the artistic impetus seems to transcend these. 'Squeezed through' is the perfect description. *Chimes at Midnight* barely got made.

The dialogue is beyond 'in the style of Shakespeare'-- it is actually Shakespeare! And one of the reasons I love it so much is the nearness of the adaptation.
